20th People's Majlis

People's Majlis

People's Majlis Committee Minutes

3rd Meeting of the Environment and Climate Change Committee

5 May 2026

Venue of the meeting: People's Majlis, G (Committee Room 5)

Time started: 11:00

{Presiding: Chair of the Committee; Member for South Maafannu constituency Abdulla Rifau}

Speech from the Chair:

بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم. I welcome all members to the third meeting of this session of the People's Majlis Environment and Climate Change Committee. The meeting is now being held in Committee Room 5. Today's date is 5 May 2026, Tuesday. The time is 11:07. On today's sitting is a meeting with Riyan Private Limited, as that party has requested to meet the Committee in connection with the survey being conducted by Riyan Private Limited together with UNDP under the name "Public Perception Survey on Climate Change and Environment Right in the Maldives". Accordingly, I invite the participants from Riyan Private Limited to be brought into the meeting. The members of our Committee present at this meeting are: Member for South Maafannu constituency Abdulla Rifau, myself; Member for Mulaku constituency Ibrahim Naufal; Member for Central Hulhumale' constituency Abdulla Shazeem; Member for Mathiveri constituency Hassan Zareer; Member for Hithaadhoo constituency Mohamed Siruhaan; Member for Gemanafushi constituency Asadhulla Shihab; Member for Vilifushi constituency Hassan Waheed; Member for Keyodhoo constituency Mohamed Niushad. So, at this point I invite the representatives of Riyan Private Limited.

(After a short while)

Assalaamu alaikum. Yes! Today's meeting was arranged because you, on behalf of Riyan Private Limited, requested to meet this Committee in connection with the survey being conducted together with UNDP. Participating in this meeting on behalf of Riyan Private Limited are Head of Research Aneesa Yoosuf, Senior Research Officer Eema Asim, and Senior Socio-Economic Research Officer Mohamed Riudha. I welcome all three of you. Here with us at this time on behalf of our Committee are: Member for South Maafannu constituency Abdulla Rifau, myself; Member for Mulaku constituency Mohamed Ibrahim Naufal; Member for Central Hulhumale' constituency Abdulla Shazeem; Member for Mathiveri constituency Hassan Zareer; Member for Hithaadhoo constituency Mohamed Siruhaan; Member for Keyodhoo constituency Mohamed Niushad; Member for Gemanafushi constituency Asadhulla Shihab. So, at this point I give the floor to the representatives of Riyan.

Head of Research of Riyan Private Limited, Aneesa Yoosuf, speaking:

Thank you for giving us a little time. To begin, I will give a little information about the project. This is a project that UNDP has assigned to us at Riyan Private Limited. The main objective of the project is to clarify how the community views, what exists in the community regarding, climate governance and environmental rights. To look at the community's perception. In carrying out this research, this study, we have conducted a survey with various individuals in the community. In addition, we are also collecting information from various relevant government offices and NGOs about what the biggest environmental, or climate-related, challenges currently faced are, what work is currently being done, and matters of that kind. Accordingly, we wanted to meet this committee of the Majlis as one of the meetings with our stakeholder list, or among the government offices we wanted to meet. I have some questions. Before going to the questions, does anyone have any question for us about the project? I will continue. First of all, could you briefly tell us, could you briefly summarise the work of this Committee regarding these environmental matters and these climate changes, the work you do.

Speech from the Chair:

Thank you. As you said, our Committee's mandate is drafting laws related to climate change and the environment, bringing the changes that need to be made to those laws, taking the lead in looking into the various matters that arise in this connection, and, along with that, looking into the various issues sent from various sectors, from government ministries, from individual members of the public and from island councils, and working to find solutions to those issues. So that is the main mandate.

Head of Research of Riyan Private Limited, Aneesa Yoosuf, speaking:

At present, what kind of legal work is being given the highest priority in relation to the environment or climate change, what is the Committee doing at present?

Speech from the Chair:

At present, in the Committee, we are doing work on looking at the extent to which the Climate Emergency Act is being implemented. That work had almost reached the stage of issuing a report. The outcome we are getting from it is that, in reality, the work under that law is not being implemented in the most desirable way. In that, the relevant institutions, or the Environment Ministry, said that very major changes need to be made to that law and that those changes would be sent to the Majlis very soon. Many of those who came said that the law the Ministry sent was changed very substantially by the committee that was here [unclear] before the law was issued. And that in our country the institutions are not even ready to implement that law. And that there are also very large budgetary constraints. So that is the kind of thing in it. Then, during this term, what came to us was to bring changes to some of the time frames in the Water and Sewerage Act. That is, a date had been set by which sewerage, water and sewerage, would be established. However, the government could not do those things by that date, so they gave a new date for it. Then, among some of the work we were able to do, where some things of the councils were not in order, there were difficulties caused by not getting the electricity, water and sewerage services needed for some government housing projects; we brought in the relevant institutions and have now resolved those matters in two places. Thank you.

Head of Research of Riyan Private Limited, Aneesa Yoosuf, speaking:

Yes! Thank you. When you mention the Climate Emergency Act, the laws that exist now, there are mainly two laws, right. The emergency law, the climate emergency law, and then the Environmental Protection and Preservation Act, right, mainly in relation to the environment. These two laws and then

then if we also look at other supplementary regulations, does the Committee believe that the current laws, or the legal framework, is enough to resolve the environmental issues faced by the Maldives?

Member for Mulaku constituency Ibrahim Naufal speaking:

Yes! Thank you for the opportunity. Yes! Laws and regulations are things that we too must change as times change. Previously, 13 [unclear], the laws and such were designed to fit that. Now, in the 20th People's Majlis, as times change, as much research is done abroad by scientists and various people, we are coming to know that such and such a thing, such and such a substance, such and such a product, such and such an item, is causing harm. And based on the studies being done, we are coming to know that if this is left entirely like this, its effects fall on our lagoons and the life in the lagoons and in various other directions. I mean taking that into consideration [unclear]. Accordingly, I believe the Emergency Act, the Environment Emergency Act, and the laws that come under it, still need to be revised. And we are bringing those revisions in consultation with stakeholders. One of the biggest responsibilities of the Environment and Climate Change Committee, of this committee of the People's Majlis, is not to go exclusively toward the environment either. We hold a very balanced stance. Within that, we have to consider that this is also a place where we humans live. We have to live too. We have to fish too. It is by fishing and eating that we stay alive. So, we have to hold all of these things within a limit, everything. Accordingly, in the environment too, plastic items are not something we can stop all at once, from today to today. We too have to survive. So, in a way that does not cause difficulty for businesses, the public and other parties, the laws even now provide for phasing out gradually

the plastic items. Among those, a complaint has also come to this Committee recently that there are some essential plastic items. For example, say, some serums used for cosmetic purposes, some travel-size bottles used by babies, and so on; there are goods that cannot be kept unless packed in a small package. That is, more of those things, in a bigger packaging, 500 ml is now the allowed size, right. Higher ml than that, I mean, putting those things on the market packed in a packaging larger than that, we see as a waste, as in reality they end up unused and wasted even by the time their shelf life ends. So, based on the differences of opinion in these matters and the consultation being held with stakeholders, we are considering whether these things can be redesigned and drafted again in a way that does not harm the environment but also does not harm the economy. Then, the laws, based on the insight we get from this and all of that, God willing, in our thinking, even now, as our Chair said, a report is being prepared on the extent to which the laws under the Climate Emergency Act are being implemented. In that there are some dissatisfactions that we too note. So, God willing, we will bring some degree of changes to those things too in the future. So, overall, if we say it, changes will always come to laws. So, God willing, in the future, in this Majlis, we will bring the amendments that need to be made to laws so that they fit today, for today, for this century, after talking and consulting with stakeholders, through consultation.

Head of Research of Riyan Private Limited, Aneesa Yoosuf, speaking:

When you mention reviewing the Climate Act, what kind of, mainly what kind of issues are you discussing now? Can that be shared?

Speech from the Chair:

In fact, the relevant institutions raise those issues when we question them in connection with these matters. So, those are issues they raise. Mainly, the way it works here is that those issues will come to this side from within the government. Rather than us taking the lead in bringing things, the main thing is to consult those institutions, have the institutions raise those issues and have them bring them. For example, if an issue of that kind comes to us from the public or from another stakeholder, we bring in the institution. We bring them in and get from them what the institution's view on this matter is and how they think it should be changed. They had said that, God willing, they would send those things during this term. Now the Ministry's mandate has also changed to some extent again. At the same time, we too are concerned [unclear] now that the EPA no longer exists as a separate institution. So, they need to bring changes to those matters too within the legal framework. So, matters of that kind. At the same time, when you mentioned earlier, some important laws were not identified, so to speak. That is, there is also a law specific to water and sewerage. A law specific to energy. And at the same time, to regulate these matters, there is also a law on the Utility Authority. So, while the Constitution in fact guarantees these rights very well, these laws mainly oblige the State, the relevant institutions of the State, as to how those rights are to be carried forward. So, the way those things are to be carried forward is very detailed in these laws; if I put it overall, the laws are sufficiently good. Then, as our Deputy Chair noted earlier, in some of these laws there are things that are difficult to implement today and in the current state of the country. How shall I put it, there is a zeal, a spirit, to do it at the level practised by the big developed countries of the world. However, even if that spirit exists, a law must be made and kept based on that country, that country's situation, the economy and all these things, if it is to be implemented. Otherwise it is not something meaningful. For example, three years after the Climate Emergency Act came, roughly, not even 10% of what is in it has

been implemented. And the regulations needed for it, the way to do it, have not been made either. So, it shows that even though the law exists, the parties who made the law at that time did not have much interest in implementing it either, or it is also seen as laws that came from some kind of third-party influence. And along with that, as I said, when we spoke with the institutions in connection with that law, the relevant technical people of those institutions say that it was not passed by the Majlis committee the way they sent it. They say that many things that were not in it were put into it by the Majlis committee. So, that is the contradiction here. Now we, this committee of this Majlis, certainly believe that we are here to help the relevant institution do what it wants to do. To set those principles. However, it is in no way our aim to make a law here that makes things difficult for them so that it is not implemented. So, we will work to see if those matters can be resolved in the way the relevant institutions see fit. So, in those matters, they also noted at that time that the Special Envoy on Environment was not something that existed when they sent the law here. Moreover, here we must very much look at the fact that this country is a country that has an Environment Minister. When a special ministry has been designated for that, having a separate Special Envoy within the President's Office to advise or give views to the President is, to me personally, at my personal level, not something I can accept at all. That is, a person of the President's, the Cabinet Minister for Environment too. Having another person appointed between that and the person in office is something I personally believe would very much give rise to a conflict of interest. This is not necessarily the view of the whole Committee. Rather, this is just my own view. So, I believe some things of this kind are not right. Where some countries of the world have put these things into such laws, those countries do not have a minister directly dedicated to the environment. In that case, having such a person to specially advise the President on this, on climate change and environment, is a good

thing. However, here, while a separate ministry has been designated for that and a separate minister is in office, if another person is in between, a conflict of interest arising between that minister and that envoy is very possible. So, some things of this kind need to be resolved within this as soon as possible. At the same time, I do not yet believe that in a developing country like the Maldives, making a carbon budget and bringing controls within that budget, things of that kind can be done in this country. For example, if a resort is told that its carbon budget is such and such an amount, then in situations where, among some things that must be done in that resort during that year, that resort's carbon budget has to be overridden or exceeded, it will become a very big difficulty. Moreover, this has to be brought to this Majlis and passed every time for things like this to be done. So, that does not yet seem to be such an easy thing for this country. Then, as our Deputy Chair noted earlier, there are still some conflicts as plastic, single-use plastic, is being phased out. In that, there is already a commercial issue with us, a discomfort raised by businesses. We are looking into that issue by talking with the Environment Ministry and the Economic Ministry, to see what middle solution can be found for it. That too comes to us in these developing countries in these matters. Even now we have a complaint that has come about trees being cut in Vilimalé. We have now sent it to the relevant institutions to get information on how that matter is proceeding. Then, when that comes, in that too, for example, if the development project in Vilimalé cannot be carried out without cutting the trees there, then the conversation has to be with the ordinary citizens there. Is it important to them that those trees remain there, or for them to get housing; challenges of this kind come up in a small country like the Maldives when going into matters of this kind. And in this, from both sides too. Now, to some extent, the Ministry has also made an announcement publicly, or there was a tweet from the Minister recently. That they are carrying out work to rephrase or redesign it in a way that causes the minimum possible harm to the trees. Then, when that comes in an official capacity

to us at the Committee, only then will we know how the Committee will decide on it. Challenges of this kind exist. And at the same time, for example, starting reclamation without building a bund wall in places being reclaimed, some places, is something that concerns us too. We too raise concerns of that kind with State ministries in such matters, saying that even if you have to start quickly, even if, for example, the EIA has not been done in the most complete way, complete basic things of this kind before starting. Then everyone will benefit more from it. Commercially too the benefit will be greater. The point is that if sand is dumped there without building a bund wall, that sand too eroding away is something that will cause losses commercially as well. So, in matters of that kind, we too raise those concerns. However, as our Deputy Chair noted earlier, within our middle ground, looking at the situation of this country, at the country's economy and all these things, things are not such that we can go exclusively for the environment and proceed in that way. So, nevertheless, in the special matters concerning the environment, we too are continuing to do the work we need to do to hold the government accountable to the maximum in those matters. Thank you.

Head of Research of Riyan Private Limited, Aneesa Yoosuf, speaking:

Thank you very much. You just mentioned the various offices that do environment-related work. What I want to ask now is about the coordination and capacity of these offices. Now the Ministry, the Environment Ministry, then the ERA, and in addition, councils too probably do some kind of work to some extent on environment-related matters of their islands or of their area. How do you see the level of coordination of the various offices related to the environment? The level of coordination.

Speech from the Chair:

All offices give very full cooperation to us, to this Committee. That is, as I said earlier, we have resolved an issue of Vilufushi. And at the same time, in a complaint that came here from Kolhufushi Council too, in that we brought all the institutions to one table, looked at how those matters had proceeded among those institutions, and found solutions to those matters. So, from this Committee, we, to any government office, and private NGOs and UN agencies, and some other NGOs that operate in other matters, for example of other parties, for example W- too; the Westminster Foundation for Democracy, they too give us very good cooperation. So, what I would say, and along with that, what I note is that in the Environment Ministry's Climate Change Department, especially the people there, very high competence in this field, a lot of energy, was noted. That is, I had the opportunity to participate in the most recent COP summit. Then, when I worked with them, having seen very closely the extent to which they have got into this matter, their dedication to it and the time they gave, I truly appreciate their work. That is, people who entered the conference at 9 in the morning were able to come out at 11:30, 12 at night. Moreover, their accommodation this time, at the most recent summit, was in a very distant area. Moreover, it took an hour and a half's drive to get there. So, they, so to speak, kept working for about two weeks without even getting sleep. So, what I note is their dedication and how they worked with great passion [unclear] for this matter. So, what I would say is very; and at the same time, we get very full cooperation from the LRA [unclear] too if we request something. Moreover, we also get cooperation in matters where we, in our capacity as members, request their cooperation in matters that arise. So, what I would say is that the cooperation of the institutions related to this matter is fully received. Then sometimes, in some matters, things do not happen because of budgetary constraints. However, even with budgetary constraints, from within the government, when we bring

those matters to the attention of the President, I would very much like to note that he too gives full cooperation in those matters.

Head of Research of Riyan Private Limited, Aneesa Yoosuf, speaking:

So, you said the technical capacity of the people at the Environment Ministry is very good, right.

Speech from the Chair:

Personally, as I said, I had the opportunity to work with the Climate Change Committee and the people of that department. I certainly learned a lot from them. At the same time, looking at the talks they gave and the presentation they gave in some sessions, it is noted that they do have the capacity. Capacity must always keep developing along with the matters of the time. So, to the extent that they get opportunities at those conferences, they too will get that development. So, whenever we meet UN agencies and other agencies, we always request capacity building for the Environment Ministry and also for this Committee of ours, and recently we have been talking with UNDP and, with their assistance too, we were able to hold a workshop. And very recently we met the Indian High Commission. We are now doing work with them too to increase the capacity of the members of this Committee, to increase it within this field. And I am certainly not an expert in this field. It is a field I have newly entered. So, I too am learning. So, I too am working, as much as I can, meeting those people outside too, and in various matters, in issues that come here too, we consult them outside in an informal capacity too to get their views on these matters. That is because, as I believe,

this is a very technical field. So, if we do it without seeking the views of people who know this technically, the harm that results from it later will be much greater. Only they will know this

view, this is a very technical field. So if we act without seeking the views of people who know it technically, the harm that results from it later will be much greater. They are the ones who know how these things will be implemented and the challenges involved, especially in a small country like the Maldives. So in my view, those who do not know should always go to those who know; that is how it has to be. It is not something we should be ashamed of either. That is why, as I said, we talk to various people and see whether we can get their help. We also try as much as possible to secure opportunities for committee members to take part in conferences held abroad. This was also the first time the committee had the opportunity to take part in a COP summit. So we hope the committee will get an opportunity at every COP summit that is held. Thank you.

Riyan Private Limited Head of Research Aneesa Yoosuf speaking:

Yes! I said that because I wanted to move to the other part of my question. How is it in terms of finances, or if we look at human resources, are any difficulties noted in these institutions working in the environment sector?

Chair speaking:

Overall, these kinds of fields are fields in which very few young people are involved and in which interest is also limited. So, as far as I can tell, they face challenges in directly recruiting technical people. Along with that, the problem that arises is that when the government secures opportunities for these young people and they develop technically, they do not get the financial benefit they expect within the civil service structure, and so we very often see them moving elsewhere. Even in UN agencies, when there are projects specific to this, the ones there are the same

people. So at the end of the day, one of these young people, and I don't know, it is quite possible that the two of you, or even all three of you, have at times moved over from somewhere else in the same way. That is very understandable for your own career development too. So it is noted that challenges of that kind come into the ministry as well. That is not something for which a solution can be found by itself, even if the ministry alone wanted it or even if we in this committee wanted it. It would have to come within the budgetary constraints, into the structure of the whole civil service. So in my view, in some technical areas, given the limited resources the country has in these people, or given how few of them there are, I believe there will be some changes that can be brought within the government system to hold on to them, by creating such technical posts separately and setting the salaries expected for them. I think some such things already exist to some extent within the civil service. For some areas such as IT, special posts have now been created with reasonable salaries. Then, as far as I know, nowhere in the world does a whole civil service system make an offer equal to what is given at corporate level or by UN agencies. So that challenge exists. So I know the government ministries will work to find solutions to it. And we in this committee will certainly give whatever support we can in that matter. Thank you.

Riyan Private Limited Head of Research Aneesa Yoosuf speaking:

I will move on to the next part. What I wanted to ask is about the extent of community participation, the extent to which community participation is included in environmental matters, and the level of awareness of environmental matters in the community. The committee oversees environmental matters, or the work various institutions do related to the environment, right? What do you think, as you see it, is the level of awareness among the public about the environment or about climate change?

Chair speaking:

In my view, from what I know, or looking at the parties we have met, awareness is noted to be low. Especially in the area of climate change, these climatic changes and these matters, I would say it is low across the whole country. Take plastic bottles, for example. Everyone knows they cause harm. But I believe the reason they are still not disposed of properly is that people do not accept how great that harm is. There are two parties in Malé working on this collection. And when WAMCO collects waste, they also advise people to pack single-use plastic separately. They and these associations are linked in the collection of these items. Even so, few places still do it that way. Along with that, some schools ban bringing in plastic. But I do not believe the children understand the direct reason for it as well as they should. Some schools also collect plastic in a way that gives the children certain awards for it. Even so, I am still not convinced by that reasoning. My own children certainly do not know the reason as well as they should. Even so, those children also take plastic to school. But it is their father or mother who collects that plastic for them. So there is a problem there. So I complained about it to that school's principal too. In fact, I am the one who has to deal with this plastic; our household is not one that creates plastic. What I mean is that we use filtered water. So we would not have single-use plastic bottles. Still, there would be bottles of some laundry detergents and things like that. So the point is that it is created, and what is wrong is that it does not come to the child on their own, when walking along the road, that if they see a bottle, for example, they should pick it up. This actually needs to be made understood by children from the very youngest age. Erosion and the dangers in it, cutting down trees, harming trees and plants and things like this, trees

and the importance of planting trees: they really do not know these things, and I notice that; my own children certainly do not know it all that well. And I cannot say how other children are. I can only speak of my own children, so I start from there. So overall, what I notice is that awareness of this has still not reached the level it should. Very many NGOs also work on this, trying in various ways to create awareness. For instance, in connection with the Addu bridge project that came to this committee, they shared things about a survey they carried out on that island. Even so, I would say that even there, that information has still not been shared with most people, with the many people who need to know it. Because it is not, the talk about it still goes, for example, OK, as they put it, people don't want it. But politically, what we see is that people still want it. So isn't there an information gap here? So it is when it is politically taken to the point of a no that it actually turns into a no. It would be a challenge to stop a development project because a group of people say no, because only a small group of environment activists say no. So I do not believe that awareness has been created to that level. So, from what is discussed by the people I have come across, what I notice is that public perception on this is actually not unanimous either. Then there would be the different view of the few people who are devoted to this, devoted to the environment. Very different indeed. For them there is nothing else. But that is also not a decision that can be made given the situation of the Maldives. So in that way, what I notice is that awareness is low.

Riyan Private Limited Head of Research Aneesa Yoosuf speaking:
Yes! Thank you. Our study also largely shows that this issue mostly comes up when the person has suffered some kind of harm. Then also how it, people often do not know how to link that issue, the problem they face, to the environment. Or often to climate change, they do not make that

connection, right, most of the time. Now with island erosion too, when the island erodes near someone's house, they take it up as an environmental issue in that sense. But the relationship between climate change and island erosion is still not known to many, right? That is the kind of thing our study also shows. Then, on the information needed for public awareness, the ministry, for example, runs a great many awareness activities. NGOs also run a great many awareness activities. Do you think there are difficulties in delivering that information? Or do you think the way it is delivered is not good? Why do you think awareness remains at such a low level after so long? It has been a very long time, right, that various parties have been working to raise awareness.

Chair speaking:
I strongly believe that it will only come if it is created, or instilled in the mind, at school level at the youngest age. So the point is that it does not run through the system at that level at the youngest age. I think when we were young there was even a subject called Environment. I wonder whether it still exists now. Called Environmental Studies. I think when we were young there was a separate, special subject called that. Environmental science. I don't think there is one now. For example, I think we must have learned some things from it too. So it is clearly noted that such things are few today. And as you said, in a place, the people of an island too only consider the island to be eroding when it reaches the point where their own house falls. Even if the other side erodes away completely. It is none of their concern. It does not become much of a problem. But once the erosion reaches their house, that is when they get worked up. So along with that, when sand is taken from the nearby lagoon, for example, they do not consider the harm that could indirectly come to the island from it, for example. Sand mining and things like that have been left by the councils too in a very careless way. Then plastic bags, for example: when a tax of 2 rufiyaa was first levied per bag, people raised very big concerns, saying a large amount was being taken as tax. But now who cares, plastic

bags. People will talk about 2 rufiyaa. So the 2 rufiyaa is not what matters here. It is not the tax. The point is that awareness of it has to be created and the habit has to change into a culture of repeatedly carrying that bag. That does not happen. At first, I think people even went around with bags under their arms because 2 rufiyaa seemed like a lot. I did too. Now, hmm, it is that so-called cloth bag now. In fact, as I see it, it is the businesses that now profit from it too. Something they used to give away for free has now become a way for them to make money on a business basis. They now sell cloth bags too, priced at 2 or 3 rufiyaa. They do not have to pay tax on that. They collect that money from the customer. So if that is the case, then even through the introduction of this tax, rather than the state, or than the environment protection levy, or even if it is later put into a green tax, at the end of the day, rather than something the state benefits from, what the citizen pays here goes to the businessman. So if that is the case, in my view its purpose is not fulfilled. So rather than this happening through the tax alone, I think a large percentage of the revenue received from the tax should now go towards creating awareness. For example, there are some islands which, even if not because of awareness, but because of some smart businesses there, have shifted very substantially to solar. From the information I know, in that place it was actually because of a smart business. He convinced people that this was something that could be done at very low cost, through various schemes, schemes that now exist within the systems. Many people do not know these exist either. To get green loans, for example, even at BML there are some funds of that kind. So many people do not have an option to access it, or a way to access it. But when this smart businessman brought it along with that option, when he installed it very easily for them. So Maldivians are actually very, some Maldivians are people who have grown used to the easy way. So it gets left like that. But if someone comes and does it for them, it is fine. So in that kind of way, for example, every single time they go to that shop, the bag they buy, inside the shop

if it could be left there and they could come back, I think that bag could be used a second time. Many things are like that. Various, very, even if we look at electric vehicles, what is the problem? In Villingili, electric vehicles are what run. That is because they are forced to. But even today, let that place be released so it is not a green zone. What I mean is, if it were released so it is no longer a green energy zone, I think the electric vehicles would all go and the whole thing would switch entirely to petrol. But the cost of that would also be high. All those harms come from it. So in matters like these, along with that awareness, Maldivians too need to bring a bit of national thinking to these things: it is each person's country. When their environment is gone, if we go under, we will all go under together. So I think thinking needs to reach that level. Then, along with that, we sometimes also see that after these things are talked about, the whole system does not act that way in practice. So in that case too, the point is that it does not add up. Sometimes, for instance, when you see the person who says smoking cigarettes is very harmful smoking a cigarette, that poses challenges to the thing. Sometimes things happen in that kind of way too. So that is what I had to say. Asadhulla.

Member for Gemanafushi constituency Asadhulla Shihab speaking:
On awareness, the question is really why people are not aware. I think that is a topic that can be discussed in a somewhat broader frame. As I see it, earlier in the Maldives, when the 2000s were starting, that is as far back as we remember, Environmental Studies was then a functional subject. Not a theoretical subject. Then in our school days, I remember, just as the Chair noted, they would take us to areas where the island was eroding, and also go and show us the diseases affecting trees, going directly to the field. The point is that Environmental Studies was a functional subject. However, over the past twenty-five or so years in the Maldives, these curricula have kept changing, changing and changing, and I don't know now whether this Environmental

Studies exists directly. But the whole thing has now become a theoretical subject. When children get that knowledge about the environment from Environmental Studies, they do not now know how to put it into practice. This is a real problem, the biggest problem there is now. Even now, if you do a proper study and look, you will not find even a small number of books about the environment in the library of any school in the Maldives now. So it has been neglected to that level. It has really been neglected by the authorities. If awareness is the point here, I think the direct solution to this is to make Environmental Studies, or that component that should be a functional subject, like it used to be. That is what I see in this.

Riyan Private Limited Head of Research Aneesa Yoosuf speaking:
Yes! OK, thank you. I will move to the next question, since time has also become very short. Now there are mechanisms in place for raising environmental concerns and complaints, right, for the public to submit complaints. These include the consultations held during the EIA process. Then again, when development projects are carried out, the ministries and the parties implementing a project also meet the public and work with them at the design stage in some projects, for example in harbour projects. So how impactful are these systems that have now been established? Or are they useful, what would you call it, are they useful systems? Do the existing systems function as they should? For making complaints and then for seeking a solution from it.

Chair speaking:
I would say the system is good. The public consultation process also goes ahead. So what happens in a public consultation process is that things go with the majority. So the majority; what a minority wants can only be achieved by the majority if it is made understood by the majority. So

what comes in here is the point that came up earlier. Awareness, and what the people in the minority say may actually be a very good point. But if they cannot get the majority to understand that point, things will go the way the majority decides. So along the way, there are situations where decisions are made in a way that is sometimes least suited to the environment, or not the most beneficial to the island, for the benefit of a few people, who bring many others in on it. For example, in a harbour project like the one you mentioned, there have been times when, through the influence of certain businesspeople and boat owners on that island, things ended up the way that benefited them most. That may at times not be the most beneficial way when looked at from an environmental perspective, or for development, even when looked at from a long-term development perspective. So in some cases, some of these public consultation processes have at times not produced the most beneficial outcome. Even so, the process is good. The process goes in the order it should. However, in some cases, because things like what I described happened in that process, things have ended up in ways that are not the most beneficial. So we also note that the government goes to public consultation on everything during the design process. And it is noted that in some cases, because of a difference of opinion that arose after work began, the government has again stopped the work, gone back to public consultation and made changes accordingly. So I would say the process is not the problem here. It is the changes brought about among the people of an island in making decisions that often lead things to end up not in the most beneficial way. In cases where the decision is largely left to the public through public consultation, the whole design process has even changed completely. So I would note that the process works well.

Member for Gemanafushi constituency Asadhulla Shihab speaking:
Now when going to public consultation too, in public consultation the decision is largely made by actually looking at public perception, right? Then the EIA that the Chair also noted earlier

process, the issue of the bund wall that now comes up in reclamation. What everyone now understands is that putting up a bund wall is environmentally friendly. But I actually don't think it is particularly environmentally friendly. Having some experience in this field, if I may say something about bund walls a little sarcastically: whether or not a bund wall is put up, sediment still escapes. So the point here is, for example, if you pass wind while wearing trousers the smell still spreads, and if you do it without them it still smells. But doing it without them is just a bit messier. That is what happens there. Actually, sediment cannot be controlled by putting up a bund wall. And when a bund wall is put up, the sediment that escapes plus the damage done to the reef is a considerably large damage. Then the sediment issue there is the escape of sediment. Is the escape directly something that destroys the reef? I don't think anyone in the Maldives has done a study on that. But from my experience I would say that when reclamation is done, the sediment settles with the current, and as it settles on the reef with the current, it is not something that stays fixed there. So as the Chair noted, putting up a bund wall is now a commercial thing. It is not something beneficial to the environment. It is something done to pour sand and contain the sand inside. So really, when we raise an environmental issue here, even when we raise an issue about a reclamation project, everyone will say the sand is being poured without putting up a bund. And to everyone, not putting up a bund seems like something harmful to the environment. In reality, it is not harming the environment. But public perception, what I am saying is that what the public understands is that if reclamation is done, a bund wall must be put up to protect the environment. That is not something that protects the environment. And especially when digging over a reef, the damage from it will be much greater. The number of corals destroyed by it will also be greater when a bund is put up. So if things are to change in the Maldives now, if things are to change in an environmentally friendly way, the concept of putting up bund walls needs to change. In my view, bund walls should only be put up with geotextiles, either geotextiles or some other method that can be placed on the reef and removed afterwards, after reshaping. A bund put up by digging the reef, by excavator, digging up the large rocks on the reef, cannot protect an environment.

Then the second thing about public perception now is that when these harbours are designed on islands across the Maldives, everyone, the island's people, and the council too, holds a big meeting like this with the island's people, what is it called? A public meeting, right. After holding a public meeting, what everyone wants from it is to put up as big a breakwater as possible; that is what everyone wants. But it is not actually about solving the problem. Because the public does not know the ins and outs of this, they too want to protect the island with zero tolerance. In trying to protect the island, when a breakwater is put up around the island, or when a breakwater is put up in the middle of an island's reef, the current created when waves come in with that force and splash against those big rocks becomes even stronger. So it will again end up scouring [unclear] somewhere else, or scouring another place nearby. But what I am saying is that this thinking needs to change. That this is not the solution here. The biggest problem now faced on islands where breakwaters are put up, I think you would have more information on it than I do: the tombolo effect that comes from putting up breakwaters. The tombolo effect, I think on some island in Baa Atoll there has been a big problem like that. When a tombolo forms, a tombolo effect, the breakwater is put up because the people want the island protected by building a breakwater all around the outside. But when a tombolo effect occurs, the tombolo forms by drawing away a large part of the island. These are not things that are actually considered in the field when EIAs are done, nor by the technical people in the councils, nor by the people there to give technical advice on this. So these are things that need to change quite substantially.
